"The Basics of Stein and the History of Rota Explorations" Vol. A

In 1905, Mr. and Mrs. Rota discovered an unidentified Field. The methods of observing it lacked regularity, but it was observable under lax conditions. They named it "Over Field". With the help of a particular means, they deduced that in the Field was an undiscovered element: Ein (in honor of Einstein who published the theory of relativity in that year).

In 1910, Mrs. Rota examined and verified a stable compound structure of Elementium and renamed it "Steinium". She believed that Elementium existed in Over Field in the form of solid gas. When she acquired a certain amount of Elementium through a particular method, it was compressed due to the different laws of physics and reacted with other elements in the air, stabilizing its structure and turning it into a crystalline mixture. Therefore, Mrs. Rota named the compound produced by Elementium reacting with other elements Steinium, and the crystalline mixture was named Stein Crystal.

In 1916, after Einstein proposed the hypothesis of a finite boundless universe, Mrs. Rota published her quantum entanglement theory "Rota Unwrapping (RU)", displayed a report on her discovery of Stein Crystal and Elementium, and read her research paper entitled "The Compressive Reaction Between Elementium and Its Compound Under Space-Time Curvature" at a conference in the International Physical Society. Rota Unwrapping, aka the Luik method, makes it possible to conduct a quantum switch in Over Field, allowing Steinium to be used as a substance in a lab.

There are still many uncertainties about Over Field. Currently, it's a consensus in the scientific community that the Over Field is from a certain part or dimension of the universe, and the Luik method is a way to create a wormhole leading to it.

"The Basics of Stein and the History of Rota Explorations" Vol. B

In 1932, Mrs. Rota passed away. Fifty years after that, her lawyer's office declared that her assets would be handed over to the Scientific Society she was affiliated to when she was alive. The Scientific Society sorted her manuscripts and discovered her unpublished theoretical paradigms of Unwrapper and "Helen Stabilizer". Unlike the theory of the Luik method (only capable of small-mass synchronization), an Unwrapper can synchronize a larger amount of quantum (about the weight of a human being), which makes it theoretically possible for humans to enter the Over Field.

As we know, Steinium, unlike any other alternative energy in the market, spontaneously returns to the Over Field after being consumed, causing no pollution whatsoever. It's an ideal alternative energy source.

In 1984, with the support of the Scientific Society, Dr. B founded Rota Exploration Co. We finished the Unwrapper, named it R Box, aka Luik Box, and the scale of the exploitation of the element gradually expanded. After 10 years' research and development, we finally succeeded in synchronizing the resonance between the Luik Box and the Helen stabilizer and gained entry into the Over Field.

Between 2009 and 2012, Prof. C of the Research Department modified the Unwrapper designed for humans into a platform for resonance and stabilization—ER Box (Luik Elevator). The professor also improved the stabilizer technology, connecting the energy consumption unit to the governor module with a resonance link, thereby inventing the management mode in which adventurers communicate with their Captain in real time through their Stabilizer Loops. Moreover, the professor also invented "Skycart", a more efficient mining device.

In 2020, Rota Exploration Co. was renamed Rota Future Tech Co., and its first large-scale exploratory project "Project Fields" officially commenced.

"The Ghost in Zohar" 1
By Marquet Tascombia

This is a tale I once heard. When I was in Arbun, people there loved telling children stories passed from mouth to mouth, and The Ghost in Zohar was one of them. Zohar was the name of a place that existed millenniums ago. In the story, Zohar is a place free of poverty and illness, and the people there enjoy benefits brought by a technology called "Matter". They are well-fed and well-clothed. However, the brightest light breeds the darkest shadows. Nobody knows when, but a strange black fog rises in Zohar. At first it is just a small patch, and in it is a figure that looks like a little girl. Out of curiosity and fear, the locals call her a "ghost". The ghost roams in the city. Nobody knows when or where she will appear. Things stay that way for a very long time. One day, the citizens suddenly realize that they seem to see the ghost everywhere—yes, she's been growing in numbers.

Driven by their fear, the citizens attempted to destroy her (them) with the power of "Matter", but it is too late. The black fog shrouds Zohar and permeates into people's mouths, ears and noses. Everybody becomes as black as part of the fog. Thus, ghosts are everywhere, and everybody is a ghost, which makes it impossible to destroy ghosts.

I discovered similar stories in books from other countries. An Asian student of mine gave me a mythology book titled 'Mores of Shimohara' (They call books of this kind 'local history books', but I find them no different than mythology books). The book mentions a country named 'Bigary'. In their language, the word "Bigary" also means light. In Bigary, there were similar occurrences of "miasma" as well. According to my student, the word "miasma" in his country in the olden days denoted poisonous or evil fog. But unlike Zohar in that story, Bigary was a country long tortured by war and food shortages. The people there were totally powerless against the black fog, and they soon were "consumed" by a black fog brought by a little girl.

The tale sounds like an exaggerated, distorted version of a story about a pandemic in every way.

"The Ghost in Zohar" 2
By Marquet Tascombia

Everybody knows this kind of tales are artistically exaggerated stories of pandemics. In ancient times, especially hundreds or thousands of years ago, primitive medical technologies were as useless against infectious diseases as the manuscript paper I just tore. The most primitive but most effective way was to block the paths and steer clear of the source of infection. Villages and countries severed ties with each other because of it. When the pandemic was over, many of them were found to have become ghost towns. People described the fear they experienced in the desolation as a black fog that was both infectious and destructive. How very vivid.

Out of my professionalism as a scholar, I planned to pay a visit to Kiichi Watanuki, an old gentleman researching 'Mores of Shimohara' when I was searching for delicious pork chop with rice and ramen and gathering materials. Unfortunately, I failed to find him. Almost a hundred years old, he was now living in a secluded sanatorium. Luckily for me, his student was willing to meet me, and he offered me some info sheets about the research he'd conducted with his mentor. I ran an eye over those comprehensible to me. His student was very happy that I paid a visit on this matter, and he fluently answered my questions about a couple of blurry parts in the notes. I couldn't help but admire how good at memorizing things oriental people were.

But my trip was not very fruitful. On one hand, I had trouble understanding the ancient book written in another language; on the other hand, the book contained only skimpy information about that story, without even mentioning the location of Bigary or anything about its history. After that, my whole trip was over, and I completely forgot this mission. What a poor memory I have.

Anyway, this tale, like the myth in which a brother and sister create the world, came down in both the East and the West. But I'm still confused as to why the ghost is a girl in every version of the story. If I'm to take a guess, maybe it's because in those dark ages, a girl's first period was deemed inauspicious and unknown, and a grotesque figure was the easiest image to depict and imagine, which was why the two were combined and a girlish ghost was born.

Who doesn't care about a white-dressed "ghost" of a girl?

"The First Day of April"
By Hozumi Sakura

April first is the day of daydreams. I was born in a season like this, which was why I was named Sakura. When I was little, I always went back to my hometown to see the cherry blossoms at this time of the year. My grandfather would take me up his favorite hill. Seen from a withered tree at the hilltop, the cherry trees in the villages and towns were like a pink river flowing from the foot of the hill into the distance.

The withered tree was the only one that wasn't flowering. But my grandfather said I could see the tree flowering in my daydream in this season. He said he once had a daydream like that in his childhood. When I was little, I longed for it; when I was older, I fantasized about it; now that I've grown up, I can't help feeling amazed that the withered tree is still here…

In my writing, I fantasize about the daydream I used to long for, the things my grandfather told me I would see in my every dream—towering blooming cherry trees, waterwheels turning slowly in the village, shrine torii as scarlet as always, festive lanterns and masks hanging from the racks. The gurgle of brooks, the chirping of birds, the sound of the windmill turning in the wind, and the shadows of Sunshine Dolls. Please don't rain on April 1st, because the fete is about to start in my daydream.

My grandfather and I agreed to meet at the stone lantern beside the windmill. But he won't be able to see me. It must be because he's too far away.

Under the withered tree, I met Joji Fukuyama. If this is also a daydream, it's a sweet one.

"The Last Day of August"
By Hozumi Sakura

In a paddy field, a married couple are separated. Sometimes people see the man, and sometimes they see the woman. When they see the man, he asks, "Did you see my wife? I'm worried about her." When they see the woman, she asks, "I'm looking for my husband. Please help me rescue him." What a strange couple. Can they not see each other? Do the tall rice plants block their views? Or do they exist in two parallel universes? This is generally what the story without an ending is about.

In the olden days, April 1st was the day when people removed the cotton interlayers of their clothes, which was called "Watanuki"; May 7th was called "Chestnut Flower Falls", which, as its name suggests, denotes the time when chestnut flowers fall; Jun. 1st is the day when fruits and melons begin to fall and crack, so people named it "Melon Cracks"; Aug. 1st is the day when ears of rice begin to grow, which become fully grown on the last day of August, so it's called "Ear's Birth". That's what a year in the natural world is like, a regular cycle repeating itself again and again. All animals' birth and death follow the same pattern. The world is the most intense rule follower, as it is supposed to be.

However, in April, incredible reveries are seen under cherry trees; the teenage girl who arrives at the city with the rainy season in May and then disappears; an abandoned baby found in a ripe melon; a married couple having trouble finding each other due to tall rice plants… Every one of these stories is like a frame planted into this continuous footage of a world. Thus, the whole thing becomes illogical, like a prank.

Unable to make head or tail of it, I had no choice but to put down my pen and picture the Maker playing a game like I do.

Anonymous Essay 1

I guess this is a kind of oriental culture. They always excel at miniaturizing natural scenery and putting it into a small courtyard. The positions of rocks, the shadows of the plants, and even the lighting are included in their calculation. Decorating their courtyards in their preferred ways, adding everything they want to add—why does art always involve the artist's greed? And greed is the reason why art is art. The logic of this world is always so inexplicable.

Though I put it this way, looking at those things for too long tires my eyes. The so-called "having too much to see" is a vexation I'm experiencing right now. Therefore, I find myself a large parasol. Though it's not raining, I can rest my eyes under it. You see, it also provides shelter from the sun, which makes it even better, doesn't it? The parasol is such a great invention.

To be honest, I'm a little bored with the views here. Of course, you can't deny that all large things boast a tremendous visual impact when you first lay eyes on them. You know, it's just a figure of speech. I'm not implying anything.

The girl in the fairy tale is so well-known. Maybe I should rename myself "Alice" and start an adventure.

That's a pretty good idea. It's about time I wrote a fairy tale book. A fairy tale book for little girls would be fine.

Anonymous Essay 2

Beware the water in vast places. I can swim so I don't have to worry too much about it, but surely not everybody swims as well as I do?

Unless you're a fish, of course. There's nothing a reading fish can do that I'll find surprising. But I'll still be curious. Hey, may I dissect you?

Just kidding. Biology is not my forte.

That's why I always keep a weather eye on "those guys". They always pop up without warning. I have no idea what I've done to earn their enmity. (Sighs) I should've learned more biological knowledge when I had the time.

I want to find a store.

I want to feed "those guys" like I feed fish in the river when I see them. Maybe my actions will be met with a pleasant surprise. For example, the conditioned responses of wildlife… Stop. That's what Iwan Petrovic does!

So much for today. I think I'll go find that feed store first.

Well, where is it?

"A Supplement to Customs of Shimohara" Vol. A
Written by Kiichi Watanuki / Edited by Kazuko Shimoshirohara

My mentor Kiichi Watanuki dedicated his life to researching "Mores of Shimohara", a book on the customs of his hometown. He was an important founder and developer of the local folklore studies.

After Mr. Watanuki passed away, when sorting his unattended notes, I discovered a lot of other contents that he hadn't had time to include in "Customs of Shimohara". I did a lot of thinking before I decided that the fruits of my mentor's work didn't deserve to lie unnoticed. Therefore, I compiled this supplementary book, imitating the style of writing of "Customs of Shimohara". Most of the content of this book is from the notes of Kiichi Watanuki, the author of "Customs of Shimohara". The annotations in the book are mostly Mr. Watanuki's work.

"The Sky Eyer opens on the Maturity Day. People offer a sacrifice to it. Officials inspect the ceremony. The light makes offerings to it. Music and dances are performed. The eye closes." (The original text is in Japanese and Chinese)

This is a story about a shrine in Shimohara 1,300 years ago. The shrine is said to be built in honor of the bird god worshipped by the locals. The bird god would open his eye on the Maturity Day. It might refer to some kind of astronomical phenomenon similar to a solar eclipse. Therefore, people held a sacrificial ceremony, had ritual officials conduct a night patrol (a patrol of the locals in which ritual officials patrol the mountains with torches in their hands, presumably in an effort to drive away "the evil"), and offered the god some kind of sacrifice (Light? Offerings? Or did it have something to do with Bigary?). People sang and danced until the divine eye eventually closed.

Even to this day, the locals still hold summer fetes of this kind. It's just the night patrol of ritual officials has evolved into a parade anybody can participate in, and the sacrificial segment has been replaced by a show in which a selected native girl dressed like a Saintess sings and dances. They don't remember whether there used to be a shrine like that, or which god it was built to honor, or the origins of the fete, but that's what the bloodline of culture is like. Even if the historical records are gradually consigned to oblivion, the customs passed down from generation to generation are still the culture itself as well as the reason why they can survive the passing of time.

"A Supplement to Mores of Shimohara" Vol. B
Written by Kiichi Watanuki / Edited by Kazuko Shimoshirohara

Documented in "Oriental Jottings" is a story about an emperor preventing infectious diseases.

"The emperor departed from the imperial city, encountered a miasmal fog and developed Ghostly Sickness. Nobody could cure it. Japonica happened to be in full bloom at that time, which healed the emperor."

The Miasmal Ghostly Sickness mentioned in the story was very similar to the pandemic in Bigary mentioned in "Mores of Shimohara". The story of Bigary, however, mainly tells of how Bigary was destroyed by the pandemic.

I analyzed the connections between the two stories in my book "Olde Tales of Tsubaki Hill". As chance would have it, Mr. Watanuki, who spent decades steeping himself in folklore studies, also included this in his notes. His speculations about the potential connection between the two stories lasted intermittently for many years. He had frequent queries about it even after finishing his book "Mores of Shimohara". He considered the possibility of japonica = Saintess, and the possibility that the story of the emperor might be a sequel to the story about Bigary, but he also suspected that the two events might be totally unrelated, because the location of Bigary was still unknown, and it might not necessarily overlap Shimohara.

What he gave the most thought to was the possibility of japonica = Saintess. In many books on natural conditions and social customs, japonica, aka camellia, is described as a plant that can cure diseases and ward off evil. In ancient times japonica blossoms were believed to be related to the sun and Saintesses, while the trunks of japonica were made into tools or even weapons. The story of Bigary says that the crisis would be resolved if a Saintess "was offered to the Holy Tree as a sacrifice", so it's possible the emperor also used japonica to conduct the same sacrificial ceremony. Of course, a more realistic way to put it is that japonica was used to cure the illness.

"Mores of Shimohara" Vol. A
By Kiichi Watanuki

According to "Mores of Shimohara", not far from Shimohara was a place called Uehara.

"Above Shimohara is Uehara. Uehara is haunted by paradoxes, thereby unfit to visit." (The original text is in Japanese and Chinese)

It means that Uehara is a place where conventions and order are peculiar, so people cannot go there. Of course, I can't say for sure whether the words "unfit to visit" mean it's physically inaccessible or too dangerous for people to visit.

I searched for relevant information in other books and records, but unfortunately, there are hardly any historical documents about Shimohara, which was a small city located among mountains on the border between two countries. (The Shimohara mentioned here is not the Shimohara of Sōja in the present day.) Uehara, however, is a place name widely used throughout the country at different times. In the Edo period alone there were at least 3 places bearing this name. But they were all far from the Shimohara in ancient times.

After giving it some further thought, I find it very difficult to tell from "Mores of Shimohara" whether that place was named Uehara after Shimohara was built, or the locals' ancestors discovered Uehara and then named the nearby place Shimohara. Therefore, we'll have to wait until more historical records are found. Maybe then the truth of this legendary place will be revealed.

Shimohara is my birthplace, which is why I dedicate myself to researching books on its natural conditions and social customs. I've always been curious as to what our ancestors went through, and what influence it has on our current lives. Although the ancient stories of "Uehara" were not passed down, I might have been to that place when I was little.

"Mores of Shimohara" Vol. B
By Kiichi Watanuki

Documented in "Mores of Shimohara" is a story about a statelet named Bigary in ancient times.

"At that time there was a country named Bigary. Lack of food led to war. Prayers were said, and Saintess of Light was demanded. Offer her to the Holy Tree, and peace would ensue. Should the Saintess return, miasma would come rising. Dark clouds descended, and evil mist arose, reducing everybody to a spectre. Bigary fell."

The story says that once upon a time, there was a country called Bigary. It's battered by frequent warfare caused by food shortages. The locals offered a Saintess of Light to their god as an offering. The crisis was resolved after they offered the Saintess to the Holy Tree. But afterward the Saintess returned, causing miasma to rise. The miasma was like dark clouds. Foul mist permeated the country, turning everybody it touched into a ghostly monster. Just like that, Bigary perished.

Similar stories are common in many countries. They're typically believed to be descriptions of pandemics or disasters dramatized to sound like legends. Back in the times when written languages hadn't been invented yet, stories were passed from mouth to mouth or through drawing. Both methods tended to exaggerate the stories to make them more entertaining. That's how those legendary tales came into being. Not until after the advent of written languages would these stories be stabilized, but by then, they might have become far removed from their original versions.

I've noticed that Bigary means light. Clearly the locals worshipped the god of light. It's very similar to Shintoists' belief in Amaterasu. Judging from the timeline, "Mores of Shimohara" was clearly finished after Shinto was founded, but even so, the author did not expressly state the origins of the belief. It's also a technique to make stories sound legendary: the further removed from our perceptions they are, the greater the antiquity they seem to have. Conversely, frequent description of what we know would make the whole thing sound more real.

"Realm of Stars" 1
By Marquet Tascombia

Like the seaweed on Takoyaki.

The importance of stars to the world can be likened to that. Lack of them won't compromise the existence of the main body, but once you've tried it, you'll discover that it's so unromantic to have no stars.

The destination of this journey of mine is an oriental island country. I haven't seen the ocean for a while now. Of course, Arbun is also a coastal city, but my house is in an out-of-the-way place and a little far from downtown.

But eventually I left the seaside and went to a mountain instead. The last time I came here, my travel companion took me to a star of this place—a local-style eatery. I'd been longing to revisit it for years. Thus, I finally got to enjoy the rice curry and ramen I had craved for so long. Pity I had to eat them alone this time. I ordered two servings as usual and kind of overate. Don't worry. I was just kidding. I finished them all.

During my spare time, I visited an old friend—I think by then we hadn't seen each other for at least ten years, ever since she got married. She and her husband emigrated to this country because of their work. The sight of her with her children made me feel they were natives of this country.

My adorable Gabby (I like to call her that, though she's guaranteed to be annoyed by it. I'll just hope she won't read this book), having gotten the stars, you're living such a happy life. I kind of envy you.

I firmly believe we came to this world in the hope of finding stars.

"A Joyous Journey to Nothingness"
By Zack

Lanterns and shakuhachi, our journey to freedom.

There's a white umbrella. Though the while umbrella is stained, it will become a good umbrella again after being washed clean in rain or snow.

The trader's ox cart was broken. A wheel of the cart rolled too fast and left its owner behind. Maybe he should seek help from the other wheel. You two need to find a way to get along.

The hide-and-seek in the village. When playing the game with the kids, I'm always the ghost. I wonder if every adult is a ghost in their eyes. But I want to be a good ghost. I think even the Buddha will smile if he hears a good ghost reciting scriptures.

I like sumo. Particularly so in summer. It feels good to bathe in the river after sweating buckets. As for the results of the game, I can't win or lose if I'm the only player, can I?

Many mountains boast waterfalls. It's said that some monks meditate under waterfalls, blending into the scenery. I haven't achieved that kind of prowess yet.

Dropping by a shrine. I walked into a shrine as if visiting a neighbor. I'm a Buddhist, while you're a servant of god. Sorry to disturb you. I didn't bring any gifts, so let me just play a tune for you. But Her Reverence the Saintess didn't recognize the tune I played. It was the chirrup of birds that I heard on my way to this mountain. She must've become too accustomed to it. How very extravagant.

Cherry Diary

Miss Kazuko said a camellia petal fell onto her notebook. Well then, what fell onto my diary was probably a cherry blossom.

It's been ten years since I transferred into the Astral Coterie, and since that chance encounter. Never did it cross my mind that I'd see her again on an island like this. She did not see me, and I just looked at her from a distance, because it was my job.

She had grown up, unmistakably an adult now, boasting a beauty I had never imagined or dared imagine. I had read those books by her, but still couldn't imagine what she looked like. Apparently I'm not as imaginative as a fictionist like her. She clearly knew nothing about the Fields, but she could always come up with stories of things extremely likely to happen in the Fields. It's truly incredible.

She's probably here to collect material for her fiction. She smilingly greeted a local government employee. She curiously photographed the shrine. She put on a mask used for a sacrificial ceremony. She enjoyed the view at the seaside alone. Was she ideating a new story?

Well, it'd be best if I left her to it as I always had.

No matter what, it's so shameful to have my real name mentioned in her novel when I had only met her once.

I never dared imagine that a teenage girl would remember me for ten years, though that cherry blossom petal had long since fallen onto my heart.

—The ultimate value of life lies in the ability to awaken and think, not just survival.

In the winter of 1878, Shelley Mary Pyrendlem was born in Marymead Town. Like most children in Marymead, she had only one place to go for education: the local child welfare group. At a young age like that, she displayed a precocious ability to learn. With the help of the welfare group, she eventually gained admission to the physics department of a state-owned university, and entered the graduate school after graduation. It was there that she met Stein Frank Rota, her future husband, and the career she would dedicate her life to: proving the existence of an unknown world and Elementium.

In 1901, Mrs. Shelley Rota and her husband Stein gained their own lab in the graduate school. They started their search for a mysterious, hidden place—the one that archaeological teams of various countries were rumored to have strayed into at that time. It was typically reckoned to be a type of mirage caused by the special structures of ancient ruins in certain locations. But Mr. and Mrs. Rota believed it might be an undiscovered world of an unknown dimension.

They spent 4 years visiting archaeological sites around the world before they succeeded in observing the Field at the end of 1904. "A Biography of Shelley Rota" Vol. B

In 1905, Mr. and Mrs. Rota deduced from the results of several observations of the Over Field that in the Field existed an undiscovered new element. As Einstein published Quantum Theory and the theory of relativity in that year, the couple named the new element "Ein". They were just about to start their research when a misfortune befell Stein.

In 1910, good fortune and misfortune paid her another joint visit. In her lab she succeeded in extracting Steinium, aka Stein Crystal, a stable compound made up of Elementium. Even to this day, people's opinions of her work are still mixed, but looking back on Shelley Rota's self-willed career in scientific research, they will see the value her life held.

"The Controversies over Artor" Vol. A
By Hawsam Hermet

Eye-shaped formation of stars, vortex-shaped formation of clouds, and indescribable aerial pits might appear in the sky. This is the mysterious part about the sky. We still don't know the regularities in the arrangement of stars, or the formation of clouds, not to mention what else there is above the sky apart from the celestial realm… But it doesn't stop people in some places from worshipping the eye-like thing as a god.

Three years ago I was dismissed from my post as an army interpreter due to lung illness. Owing to the strict quarantine regulations at the checkpoint, I had to linger in a village far away from the border. The village was built around a linden tree, which was quite common in that area. Like the residents of most neighboring areas, the villagers were all illiterate. The priory requested me to civilize the villagers. They were seen as heretics. Due to some incidents involving "witches" centuries ago, details of which were unknown, outsiders believed all members of the priory were descendants of witches, that even to this day, they were still performing eerie rituals. I'd always been interested in research on any culture, and I had worked as an interpreter in that area, so I soon found a way to communicate with them. Their traditional ceremonies were totally different from the horrifying ones that outsiders believed they were holding. My book "Apple Tree Branch" contains detailed descriptions of them.

To my surprise, it was not "witches" that they believed in. It was the eye mentioned at the beginning of this article. They called it "Eye of Artor". It forcefully reminded me of the mythology of some of the ancient civilizations I'd seen. In that mythos, "Goddess Artor" is also the eye of the chief deity. And then I discovered something even more astounding—a parchment scroll bearing an article written by a woman named Lilito. The villagers couldn't understand the words organized with ancient grammar, but it was my forte. The parchment scroll documented unimaginable history and the history of Artor. Not until I returned to the university to conduct research many years later did I learn that it was called "The Artor Problem".

"History of Radiance City"
By Hawsam Hermet

I discovered a familiar record when studying some oriental books: A nation of voodooists, born out of the morn star, their queen a high priestess, who bore the hereditary title Quietus Joy Pain. The annotation reads "The voodoo nation buried people alive at a grand ceremony, along with several others as sacrifices. Whoever returned from death would inherit the title Quietus Joy Pain."

This is an illustrated book documenting the geography of some immemorial oriental countries allegedly dating back over three millenniums. The general meaning of this passage: there was a nation worshipping the starry sky. Their queen was the highest priestess and bore the hereditary title "Quietus Joy Pain". They held ceremonies in which people were buried alive, along with several others as sacrifices. Whoever came back from the dead would become the new "Quietus Joy Pain".

In oriental language the title means the joys and pains in the afterlife. Quietus denotes death, its pronunciation similar to 'drowned' in the language. But after I had the good fortune to come by a book on the phonology of the oriental language, I learned that the word 'quietus' had another pronunciation, which was identical to the word meaning 'little sister' in the language. It also means drowned to death. But the pronunciation of the title "Quietus Joy Pain" reminds me of a very similar legend—Maraco of Radiance City.

I once read a similar legend on a parchment scroll—on the Mediterranean Sea is a small island country. It always appears when the sky glows, so people living inland call it "Glowing City". It's said that everybody in that country believes in the stars, and they call themselves "Kingdom of Stars". Their queen is the Saintess Queen, who's in charge of sacrificial ceremonies and human sacrifice. The Saintess Queen has no name. Her subjects call her Liege. And in Hebrew, the word 'liege' means 'Maraco'. I noticed that it was so similar to the oriental pronunciation of "Quietus Joy Pain".

This book features sorted contents related to Radiance City based on the historical books collected by the Academy. Should anyone find the ruins of the erstwhile Radiance City someday, please make sure to refer to this book when conducting research.

"Influence of the Folk Legend 'Lily the Archwitch'"

In the 14th century, when the plague was running rife, a woman invented a serum with the blood of someone immune to the illness and successfully saved the locals from the catastrophe by swapping their blood. The woman named Lilito was deemed a witch responsible for the plague by the then authorities, and eventually she was burned alive. This is what the story of Lily the witch is based on.

The witch legend took shape approximately in the 14th or 15th century. At that time those people she saved developed a local belief, and they spread the legend to other regions while seeking refuge, which eventually was incorporated into the local folklore. After evolving for a century or two, it became the embryo of the story we now know. The original version of the witch legend was very close to what really happened: Lilito saved millions of people's lives from demons' filth (the plague) with magic, but the authorities, in order to stay in power, persecuted her to death. Afterward, around the 17th century, a small occultism group modified the tale and added to it many elements of the folklore of other places, thereby creating the story we now know. The stories they added include "Moon Daze", "Witchy Night Travel", "Radiant Star Mother", etc.

The final version of the story is as what we know: Lily the Archwitch cures the villagers of their illness, tries to help the people rise up against their king who cares nothing about them, but is feared by them due to her immortality, and eventually is dismembered and made into a dish of immortality on the king's dining table. The story doesn't say if the king achieves immortality or not.

The twists of the plot of the tragic legend were a source of inspiration for many subsequent works, including fairy tales, fantasy novels and cartoons. But all those works are spared the gory part of the original story and end with the witch returning to her castle and disappearing into the night. Lily's kindness and tragic fate inspired many children to be nice to others. During its evolution from history to story, Lily's kindness has remained unchanged, and that's the most attractive part about the legend.

We Discuss the Motif
By Hawsam Hermet

In ancient Sumeria, there was a city named Ikilium. It's said that the place was under the protection of the chief god Nyniki. There was an abnormal astronomical phenomenon called Ikikilium, which was the origin of the city name. In Sumerian the word 'iki' means eye, and 'kilium' means flower, tree, or fruit, and 'nyn' means female ruler, monarch or god. In other words, Ikilium was a place where an eye-shaped pattern could be seen in the sky all year round, which was worshipped as a deity by the locals. Maybe because of protection from the god, Ikilium survived the Sumerian flood. Even in the times of Babylon, there were still clay tablets documenting stories of this remote little city and its divine guardian.

As chance would have it, the Hittite Empire built centuries later also left behind similar records. An eye-shaped pattern was sighted in the sky above a village called "Artora" in Carchia on a certain day, and then it started appearing at random intervals, thereby giving rise to circulation of the "Artora's Eye" legend, which later evolved into the "Goddess Artor" belief.

Owing to the systematic influence of war on mythology and religion, this regional belief gradually integrated with the mythology of the ancient civilization. Thus, "Goddess Artor" became the eye of the chief god in this mythos. Now we have a clear understanding of the origins of Artor. Artor was the result of the eventual deification of ancient people's imagination about an astronomical phenomenon.

However, not only the two rivers but also the Lindenberg region in the west, the ancient oriental countries in the east, and the civilization in the south boasting various kinds of mythos—people in all these areas shared the same belief in the Oculus. This "origin" phenomenon of people in different regions having similar cultures is called the Motif. The Motif is like a formula, one with cause and effect. And what we need to discuss is what kind of cause it is.

Refutation of the Consequentialism of Motif
By Hawsam Hermet

I still think it's wrong to expound the Motif from the outcome.

The outcome indicates that all those belief-centered cultures involving legends of the "Oculus" came into being because of people's worship of the "Oculus", an astronomical phenomenon. The cause was the astronomical phenomenon, while the effect was belief and worship. It needs to be clarified that the logic behind this cause-and-effect relationship originated from this very effect: the same traits shared by multiple beliefs.

The formation of many Motif phenomena can be deduced through this method. We might as well say that the Motif itself is an etymology generated by sorting, comparing and categorizing multiple types of similar content. However, the "Oculus" is a different case.

In fact, the research conducted in recent years suggests that many field archaeology teams sighted the Oculus phenomenon in the sky. Afterward many members of the teams stated that they had entered places totally different from their archaeological sites or experienced obviously different passing of time. Some even claimed to have seen grotesque objects. As a natural phenomenon, the Oculus displayed characteristics different from those of regular astronomical phenomena: though mirage is itself a natural phenomenon, the mirage of the Oculus has a kind of hypnotic or hallucinatory effect that makes its beholders feel as if they're really in that place.

If seen from the perspective of its effect, the belief in the Oculus is a kind of worship of an astronomical phenomenon, but if the factual events in the real world are taken into consideration, it's obviously from the specialness of this phenomenon itself. In other words, this is not a cultural Motif but a type of fact—it was the mysterious, unknown effect generated by this phenomenon that caused it to become the cause of the formation of beliefs. Its cause is not pure. If we keep trying to explain it through its effect without delving into its cause, the Oculus will always remain a mystery without answer.

From Eastern Pyramids to Western Deluge
By Hawsam Hermet

Motif is a type of theme element shared by different civilizations. It's an important "origin" in mythology, folklore studies and literature.

To put it simply, it's like the sun, which gives off light and heat and is essential to the formation and sustainment of life. In ancient times, people in almost all parts of the world worshipped the sun, offering sacrifices to it, deeming it the chief god or an important deity. Afterward, as science advanced, people came to know that the sun is a part of the universe, and so is the Earth. Thus, people gradually stopped seeing the sun as a deity and eventually accepted the fact that it's a celestial body that is beyond our control but objectively exists. But to some civilizations and people in some regions, the sun still boasts some divinity in a cultural sense. The sun is a Motif element of this type of civilization.

In the past people believed that gods dwelt in the sky where the sun was, so the sky was a realm of gods. In their eyes, the sun would never perish, so gods were immortal. Legends of edifices as high as heaven built to get closer to gods can be found in every part of the world. —If people lost their bodies and weight when they died, would it be possible for them to get closer to the sky and the sun? Thus, pyramids serving as mausoleums and sacrificial platforms were built, both in the West and in the East.

In addition, there are also stories of great floods featured in legends throughout the world. Back at the time when people were unable to solve this kind of natural disaster with levees and new river channels, floods that could destroy villages and tribes, naturally, were documented as important incidents in the early stages of every civilization. Eventually, after being passed down through generations, this Motif evolved into a variety of myths and legends, but they share the same origin.

"Witches and Moon Daze" 1
By Marquet Tascombia

Medieval moralists devised a variety of definitions of witch, all of which included a part where witches came out at night, had their magical powers boosted by the moon and then cast spells on regular persons.

After European countries gradually outlawed witch hunts, the Lindenberg area in the center witnessed an outbreak of a strange illness called Moon Daze. It's said that the patients became dazed at the sight of the moon, their eyes fixed on the moon, unresponsive to anything. When they came to themselves, they couldn't remember anything about their seizures. In simple terms, it's a kind of dementia caused by moonlight. It seemed to be a hereditary disease in a local village (my guess is that those people were somnambulists, and patients attracted to light when sleepwalking). At that time there was a book called "Witchy Disease" that documented a lot of cases of this illness. Pity the book failed to survive the passing of time. Only some books on medieval folkways mention it.

The author of that book believed that this illness was the very reason why there had been witch hunts for centuries (Because of noctambulism?). People feared those patients' behavior, so they started rumors about gatherings at night, crazy evening feasts, witches flying around at night, etc., which eventually became excuses for their witch hunts.

Of course, not all witches were female. Those male Moon Daze patients suffered similar fates. Werewolves, vampires, witches' toys, demons' puppets… Men can be protagonists of legendary tales as well—though they don't like it any more than women do.

It's really difficult to ascertain the origins of Moon Daze from books on folklore studies, because at the end of the day, noctambulism is indeed hereditary to some extent. In the past, it was not necessarily impossible for large numbers of people in a backwater to develop noctambulism. Large groups of people sleepwalking would be such a horrifying sight. It might even be the origin of those zombie tales.

"Witches and Moon Daze" 2
By Marquet Tascombia

I'm certainly aware that witch hunt was a stupid mistake—this is the basic premise of our every discussion. Now I'm ready to speechify on some topics.

Let's say those legends about witches originated from Moon Daze, and Moon Daze was indeed caused by the "magical powers" of moonlight (otherwise there would be no way to proceed with the discussion), which means the witches harnessed the powers of moonlight to perform their sorcerous rituals. It's all because of moonlight. Therefore, the witches were exposed, arrested and tortured indoors during daytime, when they had no access to the magic of the moon. It all seems to make perfect sense. But even so, people successfully burned the witches at the stake at night. Did the moon lose its magic at that time? I mean, since they were burned outdoors, it couldn't be on rainy nights.

If—and that's a big if—if the witches were unable to use magic due to the torture, despite the potency of the moonlight's magical powers… It seems to make sense. However, the witches' companions didn't come to their rescue. Who would they be able to have a gathering with the next evening? If they couldn't even save their own companions, who could they possibly victimize? And if they couldn't victimize anybody, then people had nothing to fear from witches! In the final analysis, there was never any magical moonlight! Those women were utterly unable to perform sorcerous rituals with the magical powers of moonlight. They were just female somnambulists! Likewise, werewolves, zombies and vampires were nothing but extensions of the so-called Moon Daze (sleepwalking) and animalization paranoia. As for murder and abduction of children, infectious illness and human traffickers were more likely culprits than witches.

Branding people as heathens and destroying them with the "magic" of the crowds—humans have been practicing this "magic" since ancient times. Maybe everybody is a witch. Maybe everybody is a demon more evil than witches. Maybe.

"Witches and Moon Daze" 3
By Marquet Tascombia

There is more than one witchcraft story spiced up with night and moonlight in the history of different countries and regions, but I used to believe that the so-called Moon Daze was nothing more than a legendary tale in Lindenberg. Next up I'll share a story that I heard in Asia. It was from a friend of mine who was a local: Ivanka Dai (I usually call her Diana). She was a member of the Local Chronicle Office (a department responsible for collecting, sorting and researching documents and books on the history of the city).

She remembered participating in an archaeological dig in the desert when she was younger. In the early 20th century, that area was visited by a lot of supposed "archaeologists" and "adventurers" (I prefer to call them tomb raiders), among whom was a philologist named Wilson. Wilson's first time participating in a local archaeological activity was at the start of the century. One night, having trouble getting to sleep, he walked out of his tent and found it freezing cold outside. He was just about to hide into his tent when the sky brightened. He hurriedly looked up and was fascinated by the starry sky. He beheld a gargantuan nebula in the sky shrouding the whole desert, and in the center of the vortex was a peculiar sight like nothing he'd ever seen before. It was so astounding he could not take his eyes off it. Not until dawn did his companion spot him and bring him back to his senses. But he himself believed that it had been only ten minutes or so, and his memories of that time were blurry. He couldn't remember what had happened.

He spent the following 40 years in that desert, waiting outside his tent every night for the spectacle to reappear. The locals say he's suffering from "Star Dementia", which is a disease that causes people to hallucinate when they look at the stars. It kind of sounds like Moon Daze, doesn't it?

Diana met him during an archeological mission and had the good fortune to hear this story from him. Afterward they encountered a sandstorm and Wilson went missing. If any of you happen to have heard of this Wilson, my dear readers, feel free to share with me his stories. You know where my athenaeum is.

"Rogers Logic"
By Rogers Medical Agency

The logic of Rogers is: serve every patient suffering from exceptional circumstances and every disaster or accident victim with the most heartfelt compassion a medical practitioner is expected to have. Rogers will do everything within its power to treat them. Pathology, development and research are unimportant. We'll always put our patients' well-being first.

J Pharmaceutical Company once did the opposite when treating a patient suffering from a special medical condition. They let the patient's illness deteriorate just to observe and research the special disease, which eventually caused the patient to commit suicide after killing a paramedic. What's even more maddening is that J Pharmaceutical Company used their money and therapy hype to trick the juvenile patient's family into giving them carte blanche during the treatment. The patient's family called the police after finding out about the trickery, but the police investigation was hindered by the agreement signed by the patient's family. The latter slipped into the hospital and became temporary paramedic but eventually caused the tragic incident to happen, and the patient put a premature end to his short life.

Meta Research Center, a partner of Rogers, intervened to conduct an investigation, but pressurized by the financial backer of J Pharmaceutical Company, Meta could only verify the ins and outs of the whole thing and failed to prevent the tragedy from happening. We're indignant but powerless. There are some things humans are not supposed to do. We can't allow it.

Therefore, we've decided to expand our solicitude and responsibility for our special patients: Rogers will offer free medical treatment to patients suffering from special diseases whenever they need it. Rogers will assume overall responsibility for their well-being. Rogers will not allow another tragedy to happen.

"Genetic Awakening"
By Lileni Ariattini
Nowadays many people have developed a certain level of understanding of their past and their future and have begun to get curious about their ancestry. We know our parents and our grandparents, but what about the generations before them? Who were our ancestors? What did they do? Am I related by blood to some famous historical figure? Therefore, research fields such as genetic origin-tracing began to become accessible to the public, allowing researchers to collect more samples and at the same time offer proof to satisfy people's curiosity and vanity.

As far back as when scientific research was in its early stage, scientists discovered the two genetic ancestors of our closest relatives, which were named Mitochondrial Eve and Y chromosome Adam respectively. As genetic origin-tracing became accessible to the public in recent years, a type of special gene was found throughout the world.

The discovery came as a surprise to scientists, and they started searching in authenticated historical documents and the samples used for previous origin-tracing research. Eventually, they discovered that Lilito, a woman who lived in the 14th century, possessed the Adam gene, the Eve gene and the special gene. Lilito was the leader of a group of believers in a local belief. Some of her followers preserved her hair and blood in fabrics and metal objects, which are currently in the possession of an occultism item collector. Therefore, the scientists named the gene "Gene Lilito". Due to her identity at that age, they called her "Gene Witch".

The interesting part is that this woman not only had influence on people in her time but also has followers in the present day. Those who were found to have the witch's gene through genetic origin-tracing service began to claim to be "descendants of the witch". They even refer to that woman as "Ancestral Witch" on the Net, giving rise to a new urban legend. Some youngsters, because of genetic origin-tracing, believe that they've awakened their past.

"Gazer's Book List: Niche Fiction"
Nutjob MOOK Editorial Office

In our last few fiction segments we introduced some of the currently popular light novels and light literary works in the hope of helping players get a more relaxing reading experience in this fast-changing information age. This time around we'll go "hardcore" a little and recommend some not-so-mainstream fiction works to avid readers. Maybe one of them will be the next to find its way onto your reading list.

"Lilito's Legacy"
This book was written a hundred years ago, its authorship untraceable. At that time it was deemed some kind of occultism publicity material, but some believed that its original version was just a regular book on legendary tales. Some occultism enthusiasts revised its content and then published the current version.

The Visitor Series
A science fiction book that's not exactly niche anymore but slightly controversial. Its author Jonan Dobbs serialized his works on Sci-Fi Novels when he started his career. This book of "The Visitor" series comprises 6 chapters. The story tells of the close encounter of the ninth kind between alien creatures called "Visitors" and humans. Rumor has it that it's going to be adapted for television soon, so we added it to our list of recommendations.

"Lunar Farewell"
The cross-cultural nature of folkloric oddity fiction makes it difficult for people from other regions to comprehend the original culture, which is why Hozumi Sakura's books have always received tepid responses. The video game she scripted has become quite popular among game streamers lately, so we think it's advisable for players to delve deeper into her distinctive worldview by reading her novels.

"Domain of the He Number"
A time-travel fiction novel based on difference engines and Mrs. Rota, a scientist. It's a niche work overshadowed by numerous smash hits in the golden age of science fiction. Sci-fi readers into steampunk and parallel universes might find it worth reading.

"AS Tarot Reading"

If you've read the book named "AS Dream Book" by occultism expert Tar Tarot, you would have known that the Tarot and the constitution of our world are inextricably linked. It's okay if you never read the book. Next up I'll give you a sketchy introduction to this book on occultism.

"AS Dream Book" was written in the 19th century. Its author was a scholar named Tar. Some believe that this person was non-existent, a fabrication by an occultism group, because the publication of the book was once banned. The book mentions many abstract elements of occultism during its narration of serendipitous adventures in a dreamland, such as Kabbalah the Tree of Life, the Tarot, etc., all of which appear in physical form in the dreamland and converse and interact with us (the protagonist of the story). Eventually the protagonist's journey in the dreamland comes to an end, and the truth of the whole dream world presents itself in front of us. It is another world, one outside ours. It's our "Outland", ruled by a goddess who calls herself "AS". AS explains to us the birth of the Tree of Life, the Tarot, angels and demons. It turns out that all those things are combinations of things that already exist in the real world.

It's like we are really dreaming. Science has proved that dreams are formed by blending and reorganizing our subconscious perceptions of the world, and the goddess's name AS is derived from the English word 'as' which is used to denote 'similar to'. In other words, this book, in essence, analyzes our subconsciousness. It's a science book beneath its occultism exterior.

Therefore, AS Tarot Reading is not conducted in the form of regular divination. It's conducted by interpreting cards. It allows us to learn more about ourselves by interpreting Tarot cards and then looking for the explanation for the corresponding subconscious content in the Dream Book. This is how AS Tarot Reading works.

"Lilito's Legacy 1: The Witch's Gold"
By Wolfgang Rickey

Lilito the Archwitch, to find the "Land of the Unfinished", prepares a boatful of gold, but the boatman, coveting her gold, murders her and lets her body sink into the sea. As her magical powers disappear, the boat loaded with gold sinks. Rumors run rife about the gold and over time evolve into a popular belief that the other witches know the whereabouts of the gold. Thus the witch hunt begins.

A widow who lost her husband and child finds a small piece of gold by chance. Her fellow villagers misled by the rumors, after finding out about it, accuse her of being a witch. The seigneur intends to execute her and take her gold. The widow is waiting for death when her black sheep comes to her rescue and helps her escape from the village. The widow fears that the gold might draw more covetous people to her. She is hesitating over whether to throw it away or not when she dreams of Lilito. The Archwitch tells her to keep the gold and go out to sea to look for the "Land of the Unfinished", claiming that the place can bring people back from the dead. The widow misses her child. After waking from the dream, she decides to keep the gold safe. She feeds the gold to her sheep and hides it in the animal's stomach, thereby evading capture. Afterward rumor has it that the widow has become a witch, and the rumor lasts many years.

Some people crave the gold, and some long to find the "Land of the Unfinished", among whom is a young man named Iansod. Iansod is a believer in Yoon, the ancient god of the Night Kingdom. According to the mythology of the Night Kingdom, Yoon used to be a god of light and life. One day, Yoon left the Night Kingdom, causing night to fall and life to perish. People of the Night Kingdom speculate that Yoon went to the Land of the Unfinished. Over the past few centuries, countless warriors armed with sacred swords have set out to look for the Land of the Unfinished, and Ian chooses the same path.

One day, Ian is attacked by a black sheep. He slays it with his sacred sword. The sheep was none other than the widow's black sheep. Thus, Ian acquires the gold in its stomach. In the carcass of the black sheep is a skeleton, which can be vaguely recognized as the widow. Ian is trying to bury the skeleton when it lands on the ground and a giant flower grows out of it. Among the petals is a young maiden. Her name is—Helen.

"Lilito's Legacy 2: The Witch's Dawn"
By Wolfgang Rickey

Helen and Ian arrive at the village where the widow found the piece of gold. Due to the rumors about gold, the village has become a statelet called the Gold Kingdom. Ever since the widow escaped, people have been flocking to this place in search of gold, and over time it became a kingdom. Its king is the son of the seigneur. Fascinated by Helen's beauty, the king sends his men to assassinate Ian, but Ian disposes of them one by one. Ian exposes the king's vile practice in front of his subjects, but they refuse to believe Ian, a subject of the Night Kingdom. Blinded by their biased opinions, they launch an attack on Ian. When his life is hanging by a thread, Helen displays sorcerous powers. She summons the black sheep's ghost and throws the gold at it. The sheep's black wool begins to stretch in all directions and soon the whole kingdom is shrouded in black fog. Having inhaled the black fog, people fall to the ground one after another, and so does Ian. Helen, the one he wishes to protect, is the only one left standing. Looking at the giant eye of the spectral black sheep in the sky, he prays to Yoon the god and makes a wish.

The Gold Kingdom vanishes overnight. People from other regions flood to the ruins, seemingly intending to take the now unowned belongings for themselves. They find themselves shrouded in black fog. For some reason, when they look up and see the eye in the sky, they descend into madness as well. They begin to attack each other. When they spot Helen, they start chasing her. Helen runs as fast as she can. She asks the eye in the sky about her future and then hears instructions from the black sheep, the widow, and Lilito. Then the black fog lifts, and dawn arrives. She finds herself at the seaside, the boat loaded with gold right in front of her. The gold is still in the boat. People spot it and rush toward it. To shake them off, Helen sends the boat sailing offshore with the help of the black sheep's magic. The hysterical crowds stampede into the sea in an attempt to catch up with the boat. The team of pursuers becomes longer and longer, closing in on the boat relentlessly. Horrified, Helen watches helplessly as they drag the boat underwater. She calls to the sky for help one last time…

Thus, the Gold Kingdom is no more, only the Fog Kingdom as hushed as death.

"Lilito's Legacy 3: The Witch's Resurrection"
By Wolfgang Rickey

A traveling storyteller appears in a certain country, accompanied by a black sheep. He plucks a flower whenever he reaches a new place. One day, he is telling the ancient legendary story about the witch's gold when he is arrested and thrown into prison. The jailer tells him that all topics about witches are banned in this place. Surprised, the storyteller shares stories of his travels with the jailer. They are having a good time chatting when he suddenly fishes a piece of gold out of the black sheep's mouth. He bribes the jailer with it and is released. Nobody knows exactly when, but a new rumor starts circulating about a black sheep that is an inexhaustible source of gold… The ban is not enough to curb people's avarice. The locals let their greed get the better of them once again.

The storyteller and his black sheep find themselves hunted wherever they go. He has a hard job reaching the Fog Kingdom. On the beach is a boat, in which lies the immortal body of a young maiden: Helen. The storyteller—Ian, fishes the flowers he's collected out of the black sheep's mouth one after another. He places the flowers from different countries in front of her. Soon the boat is filled with blossoms, which then turn into something like a rainbow to enfold the whole boat. At the same time, the giant eye in the sky turns into an iridescent beam of light to flash into the maiden's body.

Helen is resurrected. She's also Lilito and the widow. It transpires that Lilito transferred her soul into the gold after her death, but the gold was swallowed by the black sheep, so she became the black sheep. When the widow was seriously ill and dying, the black sheep swallowed her too to keep her alive. After the black sheep was killed, the widow who yearned to resurrect her daughter, Lilito who wished to find the Land of the Unfinished, and the black sheep that craved to save its mistress joined forces, creating Helen the witch. Helen is grateful to Ian. Ian tells her it was a fragment of Yoon the god in the faraway Land of the Unfinished that turned into the black sheep, which helped Ian fulfill his wish of protecting Helen, and which gave Helen a new life. They will head for the Land of the Unfinished in the boat loaded with gold.

"Friendship" of the Visitor Series
By Jonan Dobbs

The story starts with earthlings' accidental reception of a signal. They receive a signal that can be decoded into words. After they decipher it into multiple languages, the Chinese word meaning "friendship" is the only comprehensible word. Therefore, in order to ascertain the meaning and origin of the signal, people start making active efforts to develop intergalactic communication technologies in the hope of receiving another signal from the sender—this project is named "Signal of Friendship". Seventeen years later, ACE, a scientific research organization established for this project, finally received another message from the same source. They decipher it in the same way but only get an incomprehensible four-letter word "AUAO" and an equally nonsensical Chinese word "Aoou".

The scientists are not sure whether their interpretation of this message or the last one is incorrect, so they assemble all researchers around the world in an effort to decipher the messages again. A mathematician divulges this matter in his research papers and it goes public. Governments and civic groups of different countries begin to hype it up, calling it a chance encounter between mankind and an extraterrestrial civilization.

Someone initiates a campaign named "Tips for ACE" on social media. A grade school student speculates that AUAO might be misspelled pinyin of Aoou, and explains the word Aoou based on the explanations in the dictionary, saying it denotes a dented blister. After learning of the speculation, Dooe, an ACE member, conjectures that Aoou is the title of the civilization that sent the signals.

Dooe's conjecture, naturally, is met with ridicule from his colleagues, but he and his close friend Reiji Muta, who's also an ACE member, create a theoretical paradigm of Aoou based on the conjecture. They are running the paradigm with a program when they receive a mysterious message on their computer. The message can be deciphered with the coding system of "friendship". It means "congratulations".

Suddenly it dawns on Dooe and Reiji that the Aoou civilization, who possess much more advanced technologies, might be watching humans on the earth like guardian angels all this time. This is the start of the "friendship" between two civilizations.

"Paradise" of the Visitor Series
By Jonan Dobbs

Dooe's and Reiji's discovery does not strike ACE as exciting. Most of their colleagues believe that they forged the third message to prove their hypothesis. The two of them are not suspended, but they are reassigned to other jobs. Indignant, Dooe goes public with the third signal on the Net. Because of that, he is suspended and put under investigation. Unable to take the paradigm data home, Dooe tries several times to recreate the charts but to no avail. The netizens discussing the third signal gradually begin to suspect that it's a forgery, which makes him feel physically and mentally drained. He's hesitating over whether to give up when he receives a fourth message on his computer: friendship.

And then the theoretical paradigm created by him and his friend is sent to his computer. Excited, Dooe tries to share the news with Reiji only to learn that Reiji has gone missing while suspended. He puts his research aside and starts looking for Reiji, but halfway through his search, ACE and some special agents from multiple countries attempt to stop him. Eventually, with the help of a mysterious person named John, he finds Reiji's fiancée May. May tells Dooe what happened to Reiji: he tried to protect the finished paradigm but was put under investigation by the organization. Some colleagues, after finding out about the paradigm, expressed their agreement. Reiji took the opportunity to build a new team to conduct research in that direction. During the submission of his proposal, all computers with data of the paradigm on them were mysteriously hacked, and the data was damaged. Afterward Reiji went missing. May was put under investigation by ACE because of it. ACE believes that Reiji hacked those company computers, but May suspects that the culprit was the one Dooe and Reiji communicated with: the Aoou civilization.

Dooe tries asking the sender of those messages on his personal computer but never receives a response. Was "Friendship" nothing but a con game? Or is ACE hiding more secrets? But no matter what, the Aoou civilization is not a fantasy exclusive to Dooe and Reiji anymore. Because shortly afterward, a fifth message in all languages appears on every website and in everybody's mind: "Paradise".

"Goddess" of the Visitor Series
By Jonan Dobbs

The "Paradise" incident shocks the world. The ACE organization, the government of every nation, and all netizens are horrified by the message sent directly into their consciousness. If that civilization really has the technology to do something like this so easily, then they can destroy mankind just as easily.

Another 8 years have passed since the fifth signal. That fear is so traumatic that people have stopped all space-related activities in an effort to dismiss it. Everything relevant to that incident on online media platforms has been deleted except for topics like "the Mandela effect", and Reiji Muta has disappeared without a trace. Dooe has now become a sci-fi writer, who writes novels based on speculations about the Aoou civilization every day to earn a meager income. In the past 8 years he hasn't received any other signals either, and the data of the Aoou paradigm on his computer has been damaged without him noticing. Dooe has lost his paradise. He writes stories only to make a living. During his repetitious daily routine, only his occasional thoughts of Reiji make him sentimental.

Things change on the day Reiji's wife May visits Dooe. Dooe has long since moved out of that city and settled down in his hometown. It takes May quite a while to find him. Her visit comes as a surprise to Dooe, because she's accompanied by another person—Reiji. Dooe asks Reiji if he has been missing for so long because ACE persecuted him, but Reiji gives him a negative answer. It turns out that in the past 8 years Reiji and May have joined a secret organization—EYES, which means the eyes of the earth. The name comprises the fifth letters after A, U, A, and O respectively and is similar to ACE. They claim to be a group that has really been communicating with Aoou. Some ACE members planned to conceal the existence of the extraterrestrial civilization, which caused Dooe and Reiji to be suspended, but there were also some ACE members opposing the decision. Those people helped Reiji continue his research. Dooe is taken to the base of EYES. After a welcome dinner and some catching up, May suddenly changes her way of speaking and tells him she's a "Visitor", and Reiji addresses her as "Goddess".

"Skydome" of the Visitor Series
By Jonan Dobbs

May is no longer the woman Dooe knows. Inside her is another consciousness. "Goddess" is a form of address used by members of EYES when they communicate with this consciousness. She doesn't seem to have a name. The Visitor says she came for their "friendship". She displays a holographic image to Dooe—that is none other than the theoretical paradigm of Aoou. Even to this day, Dooe still remembers the overwhelming thrill he felt when he first saw it. The paradigm soon turns into a more vivid model. It's like watching a planet come into being.

The visitor tells him that this is the real form of Aoou: Skydome. Skydome is described as a thin film of water capable of finite expansion. Inside the film are countless molecule-like spaces inhabited by Aoou denizens. The Skydome is as soft as a bubble, unstable and its structure can be damaged at any moment. There used to be more than one Skydome, but after hundreds of thousands of years, there were fewer and fewer Skydomes left, and Aoou residents had to seek help from friendly species on other planets, hoping that they would help them find another place to live. They called it "Paradise Project". And the paradise they eventually found was none other than this planet—the earth.

Aoou residents used all technologies at their disposal and finally found planet earth. They traveled at light speed in their minimal-structured film, and when they eventually reached the earth, they released it into the atmosphere and sent a message in electronic form, which was the first message meaning "friendship". Therefore, the information acquired by the Skydome around planet earth was transmitted to the one around Aoou in real time. "Famous Collector's Tomes: King of Book Realm"

This time around the book depository I'm introducing is located in Arbun. It was the residence of Marquet Tascombia the writer when she was alive: the Book Realm, currently known as the Knowledge Kingdom Athenaeum.

Marquet Tascombia was born in the 1960s. Her original name was Merray Lily Zohar. She was the daughter of Marquet Zohar the historian. She took on the mantle of her father's research into history and folkways and dedicated many years of her life to collecting folk legends and ascertaining their origins. Her folklore notes are of a highly individual style. In her later years, she shifted her focus to writing fiction novels, and her works were quite popular among young people.

Afterward, to keep up with the times, she began to serialize her novels online and some of her long-time readers were displeased, saying she went too far in catering to the mass-market, but we have to admit that an old-timer willing to move with the times like her deserved everybody's respect.

Of course, writing prowess such as hers undoubtedly requires extensive knowledge, which her collection of books is more than enough to provide. In her book depository, we can see many reference books on subjects she was good at: folklore, history, occultism, sci-fi, etc. There are pure reference books, textbooks, world-famous masterpieces and classics. It's said that she once lent out a lot of books, but even so, there are still a considerable number of books left.

This is the former residence of Marquet, ruler of the "Book Realm", a woman who had her own interests and followed her heart for her whole life.

"Realm of Stars" 2
By Marquet Tascombia

For example, the marks on the dial of a clock.

Like the stars, the passing of time follows a pattern, irrespective of place.

The purpose of this journey was to visit a 16th-century scholar I was interested in. His family has been studying humanity, culture and history for generations, accumulating knowledge bit by bit like the marks on a dial.

I once lost my star there… I had thought I would never want to visit it again, but it was totally different now. I could no longer feel what I used to feel in there. It was faintly regrettable that I failed to find that scholar's descendant. It's said he was working in another place, that he had only just gotten the job. Bad luck.

But I think he probably has his own star too. Because his family has always been around the same star, living out their lives step by step like the hands of a clock. How nice it is.

I once craved a life like that too, and would've still had one had I not lost it in that place.

I once said that we humans forcibly parasitize the earth like barnacles do their hosts, and it's only a matter of time before we become a threat to the earth and eventually cause its death. The [Oculus] that is ubiquitous in our world is the eye we need. The earliest historical record of the [Oculus] dates back one or two thousand years. It's older than most of our civilizations! Everybody sees it, irrespective of place and race. It used to be a universal belief. However, as religious dominion dwindled, people were [Blindfolded]. If we were a sightless species, I wouldn't be saying any of this, but we humans are clearly such an intelligent species, and yet we have ended up being blind to the truth. It's all because we stopped believing.

Believe, we can see the true world! The [Sky Eye] used to be our belief. It will surely let us see! Whatever we see used to be a part of our world!

In the olden days, the Oculus phenomenon was called the [Sky Eye]. At that time, people of a statelet named Bigary near the Misty Hill worshipped the astronomical phenomenon. They started holding ceremonies to offer sacrifices to the Sky Eye a very long time ago. Afterward Bigary perished and on its ruins rose two cities: Uehara and Shimohara. They had their own belief in the Sky Eye as well, believing that it was a giant bird god named "Sky Eyer" (some called it "Maturity Eye of Fate"), to which they regularly made offerings. Even to this day, there are still statues of this bird god in shrines in Shimohara, but for some reason, the god's name has been mistakenly remembered as "Maturity Day of Fate".

Records of the Sky Eye on the Isle of Moon also date back over a millennium. In the past, when text hadn't been invented yet, people there regarded the Sky Eye as a black counterpart of the moon. Therefore, the Sky Eye was also called the Sky Moon by the locals. They believed that "eye" and "moon" were respectively the enclosed aspect and the open aspect of the same connotation. The Sky Eye Shrine on the isle has always been dedicated to worship of the Sky Eye itself.

On the surface, these two places are unconnected except for the Sky Eye, but in fact, it's not the case. The founder of the Sky Eye Shrine was from the Misty Hill, but after the shrine was built, the Whitefog Shrine on the Misty Hill mysteriously disappeared. And now the Whitefog Shrine has reappeared, but the old Sky Eye Shrine vanished. Many of the modern objects in the shrine are from the Isle of Moon, which makes it difficult for people not to think about possible connections between the two places.

"Lunar Farewell"
By Hozumi Sakura

My grandfather was a folklorist. He spent his earlier years traveling around the country, collecting and researching local folklore, records and documents. He once told me about a place named the Isle of Eye Opening, saying that the locals annually held a rare sacrificial ceremony—Blindfold Lunar Farewell. To collect material for my novel, I decided to visit the island on New Year's Day and check the event out.

Having learned that I was here for the "Lunar Farewell" ceremony, Miss Dim, a government employee responsible for meeting me, started introducing the event to me: the words "Blindfold Lunar Farewell" mean that people outdoors on the island need to cover their eyes with their hands until the new moon disappears. Before the ceremony, a child would be selected as the Celestial Eye-Opener, who was the only one allowed to keep their eyes open throughout the ceremony. They say they need to see the new moon off, but actually, the ceremony ends when the selected child, who sets off from the center of the island, reaches the seaside where the "Eye" is, and then everybody can open their eyes. Keeping my eyes closed for that long struck me as tiring, so I started to have second thoughts, but Miss Dim told me that participants were allowed to wear masks at the ceremony. It was so helpful. The ceremony began. As nobody but the selected child was allowed to move, I decided to wait at the seaside, which was the destination of the child's trip. Wearing a mask, I waited and waited, but the selected child was nowhere to be seen. Bored stiff, I started pondering what the "Eye" was. Just then, I discovered that there was actually another full moon in the night sky! The moon was gazing at me like an eye. I was fascinated by the spectacle, as if beholding a new world on the moon…

Not until the next day did I come to know that it was an astronomical phenomenon peculiar to this island in winter, and the so-called Blindfold Lunar Farewell was derived from a riddle that went 'The enclosed moon becomes an eye'. Bright, bright the japonica, all radiant with vigor. I behold it but can't accept it.
Bright, bright the japonica, all feminine with vitality. A present of the present day.
